text.p: The following are the main stories from Tuesday's Albanian newspapers. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy:

- Investors of the Populli pyramid scheme which had its assets frozen will get 60 percent of their investments back at Savings Bank outlets on Wednesday. Bankers said investors could either choose to draw cash or receive bank certificates.
- President Sali Berisha has invited political parties to discuss measures to soothe the impact of the collapse of the pyramid schemes and the future of others.
- Opposition parties flatly rejected Berisha's offer saying they want a political, not a technical solution to the crisis.

- The paper says Berisha called the round table discussion because he has decided to close down investment firms which also run high-interest credit schemes and wants it to seem the work of his political oponnents.
- The paper published a blank page to protest against the arrest of its correspondent Roland Beqiraj who has been detained for eight days but has not yet been told what charges he faces.

- Ruling Democratic Party founder now turned trade union boss, Azem Hajdari, says union protests will escalate although police prevented supporters and Hajdari himself from reaching the site of a union rally on Sunday, arresting 19 people.

- Two more parties, the National Unity Party and the Agrarians have joined the Forum for Democracy which was founded last week by seven opposition parties and an association of former anti-communist dissidents. The forum has elected three former political prisoners to head it.
- The International Monetary Fund has told Albania to close down even the 'half' pyramid schemes, meaning the firms which also have investments besides the high-yield credit schemes.
- Four surviving investment companies have decided to slash the interest of their credit schemes.

- The Gjallica investment company, which owes investors some $300 million has declared bankruptcy, according to a source close to its president Fitim Gerxhaliu. It did not have enough money to pay its own employees.
